## Why This Is Asked

Tests understanding of 128-bit rotation, edge-case handling without branches, and safe shift magnitudes using masking.

## Key Concepts

- Bitwise rotate with shifts
- Modulo-like normalization using masks
- Safe 128-bit shifts without UB

## Code Example

```cpp
uint128 ror128(uint128 x, unsigned int k) {
  k &= 127;
  return (x >> k) | (x << ((128 - k) & 127));
}
```

Tests knowledge of bitwise rotations, a common low-level operation, and handling edge cases when k wraps around 32 without using branches. It also demonstrates how to make shifts robust against k=0 or k=31.

## Key Concepts
- Bitwise rotation using shifts and OR
- Modulo wrapping using masking and two's complement tricks
- Avoiding undefined shifts for k=0

## Code Example
```javascript
function rotateLeft32(n, k) {
  k = k & 31;
  return ((n << k) | (n >>> ((-k) & 31))) >>> 0;
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt for rotateRight32?
- How would you test boundary cases with k=0 and k=31?

questions.explanation:
## Why This Is Asked
Constant-time 128-bit comparison is core in cryptography and DB internals to avoid timing channels; probe understanding of lexicographic, boundary handling without branches.

## Key Concepts
- Branchless logic with masks
- Lexicographic 128-bit comparison
- Handling hi/lo boundaries in constant time

## Code Example
```javascript
typedef struct { uint64_t hi; uint64_t lo; } uint128;
static inline int8_t cmp128(uint128 a, uint128 b) {
  int hi = (a.hi > b.hi) - (a.hi < b.hi); // -1,0,1
  int lo = (a.lo > b.lo) - (a.lo < b.lo);
  int m = -(int)(hi != 0); // -1 when hi != 0, else 0
  return (int8_t)((hi & m) | (lo & ~m));
}
```

## Follow-up Questions
- How would you adapt this to return a sign-agnostic 0/1/2 encoding for a hash comparison?
- Could you prove this runs in constant time regardless of inputs and compiler optimizations?
